title: Prop get set decode
description:
Property Get and Property Set data payload (for each offset) was node decoded.

This is fixed as follows:
- added functions to decode the supported offsets
- the nvme rdma command structure was extended to store necessary command context. This allows decoding of status for Property Get
- Payload of Property Set is also decoded.

Based on the previous merge request. First commit starts at 2cfe476b.

Anders, sorry for the confusion with the order of merge requests. The merge request [2049](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/2049) was based on  the code changes in this request (not logically, but due to locality of the code changes, one would have to depend on the other).

I have tried to make it clear in the description of the MR 2049. You approved both MRs.

Now, the MR 2049 has been merged, and all commits were squashed to a single commit message (including commits from this MR).

The good news are, the code is in. The bad news, there is no clear commit message, and the changes are piggy-backed on RDMA tracking context commit.

What do we do now? Create a merge point? Revert and recommit as two changes? Force rebase by editing commit (splitting in two)? Or let it be?

Hi,
The traditional workflow before moving to git lab has been one MR one commit and MRs beeing independent of eaach other
or held back until the first one has been commited. I have continued in the same way and not looked to closly on the commits in an MR assuming them to be misstakes (not doing --amend) I must admit. I would vote for let it be but up to you.
Regards
Anders

Ok, thank you for your reply. I understand now the work flow logic better. Sorry, was new to this...

If I were to vote, I would like to have two distinct commits. I am just not sure of what is the best way to "edit" a commit in the master branch. I do not know if developers ever reset it, and I do not have commit rights to master branch. So that was my question.

I can prepare a new merge request that reverts the change and applies it as two distinct changes. I just hoped we can avoid revert commit in the log.

So the bottom line is: if I want to split that commit into two, shall I ask someone to reset the master branch or prepare a new merge requests that reverts and applies as two commits?

Hi,
>So the bottom line is: if I want to split that commit into two, shall I ask someone to reset the master branch or prepare a >new merge requests that reverts and applies as two commits?

Not sure not a git magican...

Thinking more about it and understanding how the collaboration and build flow works, I think resetting a master branch is pretty much impossible.

So, I have updated the branch to revert the commit and split it into two.

If you approve that, please do not join commits when merging to master -- the update only makes sense if these commits are separate (including the revert).

Thank you and sorry again for the confusion caused.

commits_data.message:
NVME RDMA dissector: store RDMA transfers and link them to commands.

Details:
* At this point works for single RDMA transfer per command
* Commands are linked to RDMA requests
* RDMA requests are linked to commands (read and only first write)
* RDMA read requests are linked to read responses (only first response)
* RDMA read responses are linked to requests (only first response)
* RDMA read responses are linked to commands (only first response)
